topic: Peptides your body makes: alpha-MSH, the skin's own tanning signal. UV damages DNA in keratinocytes; p53 switches on the POMC gene; POMC is cleaved into alpha-MSH (Cui et al., Cell 2007, via Harvard Medical School 2007); keratinocyte alpha-MSH activates MC1R on melanocytes, increasing eumelanin synthesis and melanosome transfer to keratinocytes; red-hair MC1R variants (R151C, R160W, D294H) impair signaling and eumelanin synthesis (Upadhyay et al., Pigment Cell Melanoma Res 2024; Nasti & Timares, Photochem Photobiol 2015); melanin forms supranuclear caps thought to shield DNA; delayed tanning appears 2-3 days after UV (Brenner & Hearing, Photochem Photobiol 2008)

Peptides Nepal01/07

Peptides your body makes

Your skin makes its own tanning signal.

Peptides Nepal02/07
Step 1 · Sun

UV hits your skin.

It damages DNA in your skin cells.

A guard protein, p53, notices the damage.

Peptides Nepal03/07
Step 2 · Signal

α-MSH

p53 switches on a gene called POMC.

Its protein is cut into a small peptide: α-MSH.

Peptides Nepal04/07
Step 3 · Pigment

More dark melanin.

α-MSH binds MC1R on your pigment cells (melanocytes).

They make more dark eumelanin.

Peptides Nepal05/07
Step 4 · Shield

A tiny umbrella.

The pigment moves into your skin cells.

It sits like a cap over each cell's DNA.

Peptides Nepal06/07
Two surprises
2–3 daysA new tan only shows 2–3 days after sun.
Red hairMC1R variants weaken the signal, so less dark pigment is made.
